title: Research Bite #21: Teaching with Worked Examples
author: Craig Barton
summary: Research Bite #21 covers Wesenberg et al.'s study on why the specific problems chosen for worked examples matter as much as the explanations attached to them. Across four experiments, the authors show that even small differences in which problem is used to demonstrate a procedure can make the resulting worked example more or less ambiguous, and that more ambiguous examples reliably produce worse test performance, more misconceptions, and less accurate self-assessment of understanding. A key mechanism is coincidence: when a problem's solution happens to share superficial features with its statement, students can infer a plausible-but-wrong rule, and that misinterpretation sticks even when a correct explanation is provided alongside the example. The findings also show students tend to prioritize the example itself over any accompanying explanation, so a poorly chosen example can override good verbal instruction rather than being corrected by it. For teachers building worked examples with limited time, the message is to scrutinize the specific problem selected -- not just the explanation -- because an ambiguous example can teach the wrong lesson even when the words around it are correct.
points: The core finding that problem selection, not just explanation quality, drives whether a worked example teaches the right rule or an accidental wrong one.
Students systematically prioritize learning from the example itself over the accompanying explanation, meaning a bad example isn't reliably rescued by good verbal teaching.
Ambiguous examples -- where the solution coincidentally shares surface features with the problem statement -- are a specific, avoidable trap in item and example design.

The paper's practical constraint for time-pressed teachers: when only a few worked examples can be used, the selection of the specific problem deserves as much scrutiny as the explanation written around it.
quotes: The authors argue that the choice of problems influences the ambiguity of the resulting examples, with more ambiguous examples leading to poorer learning outcomes.
Four studies are presented, demonstrating that less ambiguous examples consistently resulted in better test performance, fewer misconceptions, and more accurate self-assessment of learning.
Even seemingly minor variations in the problem statement can affect the ambiguity of the worked example, influencing students’ ability to understand the concept being taught.
Problems that lead to solutions that coincidentally include elements from the problem statement should be avoided, as they tend to be more ambiguous and can lead to misconceptions.
Teachers should be aware that students often prioritize learning from examples over explanations, even when provided with both.
